pairedDiff.explanation: Per-question comparison shows, instead of just the average, exactly which questions started passing (were bad, then became good) and which broke (were good, then became bad). The average metric can stay unchanged even when part of the questions improved and part got worse. This view shows every question individually.

pairedDiff.nothingToPair: There was nothing to pair: {{onlyA}} questions exist only in A and {{onlyB}} only in B. This does not mean the configuration change had no effect.

comparisonPage.title: Comparison
comparisonPage.whyBody: Comparing two runs answers a specific question: <0>did things get better or worse because of a specific config change</0> — not "the metric seemed to go up". The platform itself shows exactly which config fields differ, and renders a verdict (improved / regressed / noise) for each metric using the same 5% threshold the run page's automatic regression guard uses. The most reliable way to compare is to change <1>one variable at a time</1>: then the difference in metrics is explained by that variable alone, not the sum of several simultaneous changes.

means.improved: Better: {{metric}} rose past the noise threshold
means.regressed: Worse: {{metric}} fell past the noise threshold
means.noise: Barely past the threshold, no conclusion on its own
means.notMeasured: Measured in run {{side}} only, so there is no delta

empty_run.title: Run {{side}} answered no questions
empty_run.detail: It holds no question results, so there is nothing to compare against. Every number below rests on the other run alone.

different_dataset.title: The runs were made on different datasets
different_dataset.detail: A: {{dataset_before}}, {{count_before}} questions. B: {{dataset_after}}, {{count_after}} questions. The averages below are taken over different question sets.

different_corpus.title: The runs were made against different corpora
different_corpus.detail: A: {{corpus_before}}. B: {{corpus_after}}. Retrieval metrics here measure two different indexes.

no_overlap.title: No question is shared by the two runs
no_overlap.detail: {{only_in_before}} questions exist only in A and {{only_in_after}} only in B. The per-question comparison is empty because nothing could be paired, which is a different statement from a change that moved no question.

partial_overlap.title: The dataset changed between the two runs
partial_overlap.detail: Both runs name the same dataset, yet {{only_in_before}} questions appear only in A and {{only_in_after}} only in B. The comparison covers the {{matched}} they share.

different_realm.title: The runs belong to different realms
different_realm.detail: A: {{realm_before}}. B: {{realm_after}}. A realm carries its own corpus and its own backends, and it is absent from the configuration diff below.

different_prompt.detail: A: {{prompt_before}} v{{version_before}}. B: {{prompt_after}} v{{version_after}}. The prompt is recorded on the run and absent from the configuration diff, so the diff can read as identical while the answers came from different instructions.

different_generator_model.title: The answers were generated by different models
different_generator_model.detail: A: {{model_before}}. B: {{model_after}}. The model is recorded on the run and absent from the configuration diff below.

retrieval_only_mismatch.title: One run skipped generation
retrieval_only_mismatch.detail: A retrieval-only run scores retrieval and never pays for an answer, so the two runs carry different metrics by construction.

partial_run.title: Run {{side}} was stopped early
partial_run.detail: It answered fewer questions than the dataset holds, so its averages were taken over fewer questions than the other run's.

errored_questions.title: Some questions failed to be answered
errored_questions.detail: A: {{errored_before}}. B: {{errored_after}}. A failed question carries no metrics, so the averages cover fewer questions than the pairing does.

coverage_unverified.detail: Its answerability classes came from the dataset's own refs without a check against the index ({{reason}}). Which questions count toward its retrieval metrics is therefore unverified.

dumpErrorHints.qdrantSnapshotNotNative: This usually means the uploaded file wasn't produced by Qdrant's own snapshot API. Common causes: the file was assembled by copying/archiving the raw storage/collections/<name>/ directory instead of calling POST /collections/{name}/snapshots (or qdrant-client's create_snapshot()); it came from an incompatible Qdrant version; or the download is incomplete/corrupted (re-downloading a file the browser saved as "... 2.snapshot" or similar is a common way to end up with a bad copy by mistake). Fix: on the source Qdrant instance, generate a fresh snapshot via its own snapshot API, download that exact file, and upload it again.

dumpTypeHint.neo4j-chunks: NDJSON or JSON (array/single object, .gz/.zip fine) of {chunk_id, doc_id, text, structural_path?} objects. Every value travels as a database parameter, never as literal Cypher text — safe for free-form text with quotes, newlines, anything. Prefer this over the Cypher-script option above for a :Chunk-graph export: a raw Cypher dump inlines text as string literals, which breaks the moment the exporter doesn't escape an embedded quote — this can't happen here.
dumpTypeHint.neo4j-cypher: A file of `;`-separated Cypher statements (e.g. an apoc.export.cypher.all dump). Runs sequentially; stops at the first failure and reports how many statements already applied. Acts on the Realm's whole graph — Neo4j has no corpus_id partitioning.
dumpTypeHint.opensearch-dump: NDJSON file (.gz or .zip is fine — decompressed automatically): one JSON object per line (text/doc_id/chunk_id/strategy_id/structural_path/metadata — the same shape the indexer itself writes). Plain JSON (an array of objects, or a single object) works too. chunk_id becomes the document _id, so re-uploading overwrites instead of duplicating.
dumpTypeHint.qdrant-snapshot: A .snapshot file — Qdrant's own native format (produced by POST /collections/{name}/snapshots or qdrant-client). Restoring replaces the target collection's contents wholesale — this is not a merge with chunks already indexed there.
dumpTypeHint.text: Plain .txt/.md files — chunked with the selected strategy. Lay files out as <source_code>/<number>.txt to get source_code/article_no metadata for free (article references); otherwise a generic structural reference is used instead.

upload.heading: Upload files
upload.replaceNeo4jChunks: Fully wipe the graph before loading (the ENTIRE Realm's graph, not just this corpus — Neo4j has no corpus_id partitioning to scope a narrower wipe to). Otherwise chunks are upserted by chunk_id — re-uploading the same dump updates in place, but chunks missing from a newer dump stay in the graph, same as the OpenSearch dump mode's non-destructive default.
upload.replaceNeo4jGraph: Fully wipe the graph before loading (the ENTIRE Realm's graph, not just this corpus — Neo4j has no corpus_id partitioning to scope a narrower wipe to). Otherwise the script's own content decides: a CREATE-based dump duplicates on re-upload, only a MERGE-based one is idempotent.
upload.replaceOpensearchIndex: Fully recreate the index before loading (otherwise it's an upsert by chunk_id — chunks missing from the new dump stay in the index)

domainPacksPage.title: Domain packs
domainPacksPage.whatAndWhyBody1: A domain pack is a pluggable module with rules for a specific domain (question routing, answer formatting masks, source scoring, refusal policy, freshness checks). The platform core knows nothing about specific domains — they're plugged in and appear here automatically as long as their directory has a manifest file.
domainPacksPage.whatAndWhyBody2: Activating a domain for chat requires restarting the gateway — packs load once at startup, live reload isn't supported. For running an experiment you don't need to worry about activation at all — the relevant components can be picked directly in the "New run" form, independent of this global toggle.
domainPacksPage.whatAndWhyBody3: Activation applies to the whole Realm, not to one specific corpus: turning a pack on here applies its rules to every query in this Realm, regardless of which corpus_id is targeted in chat or a run. If one Realm has several corpora from different domains, there's no way to apply a pack to only one of them — it's all or nothing per Realm.
domainPacksPage.whatAndWhyBody4: The list above is code on the server, not rows in a database: this page cannot create a pack, only enable one already written. Two places are scanned — this build’s domain_packs/ and the directories named in CAUSA_DOMAIN_PACKS — and a pack carrying your own subject area lives in the latter, never entering the shared repository.
domainPacksPage.catalogHint: The catalogue is platform-wide; which packs are on is each realm's own. The core stays neutral to any subject area — a test enforces that, not a convention.
domainPacksPage.whatAndWhyBody5: A pack plugs into the platform’s own built-in pipeline: its routing, masks and refusal run inside its own RAG. It has nothing to do with an external RAG over HTTP — that system has its own logic, and the platform only measures it.

archDiagram.captionGraph: — Neo4j + Qdrant (OpenSearch is not involved). These are distinct pipelines that cannot be combined with each other.

archSection.bundledRagParagraph: The bundled RAG is a reference implementation that currently lives inside the gateway. It will eventually be split out into its own service. An external RAG manages its own resources — the platform never connects to its infrastructure.
archSection.externalIntegrationIntro: Three integration tiers, in decreasing order of implementation complexity:
archSection.keyInvariantRest: does not depend on FastAPI, specific adapters, or MongoDB — only Pydantic v2 and the standard library. This lets you test all business logic without spinning up any infrastructure.
archSection.lead: The platform consists of three layers: the client (React UI), the API Gateway (FastAPI), and a set of swappable backends. External RAGs connect over HTTP without any changes to the platform.
archSection.ragPipelineParagraph: selects exactly ONE combination of retrievers (not all at once): Qdrant only, Qdrant+OpenSearch (hybrid), or Neo4j+Qdrant (graph) — GraphRAG never uses OpenSearch.
archSection.table1Row1Role: Measurement instrument: computes semantic metrics (answer_similarity, context_support, grounded_in_correct_source). A fixed "ruler" — the same one for every RAG, otherwise metrics wouldn't be comparable.
archSection.table1Row2Role: Corpus browser (scrolling through chunks), near-duplicate detector (k-NN sampling of 300 chunks), source of source_code labels for annotating Neo4j communities, chunk collection for LLM-judge diagnostics.
archSection.table1Row3Role: GDS Leiden/Louvain community detection over the whole graph plus drill-down per community. Neo4j is not partitioned by corpus_id — the graph is shared, and corpus_id is used only for mapping labels from Qdrant.
archSection.table1Row4Role: LLM judge for deep chunk diagnostics: Ragas (faithfulness/relevance), TruLens (groundedness), chunk-coherence (1 call per chunk). Not used for run metrics — those use BGE-M3.
archSection.table2Row1Role: Retrieval embedder — vectorizes the query for searching in Qdrant. Same process, a second mode of operation.
archSection.table2Row2Role: Dense vector store. ANN cosine search over the {corpus_id}__{strategy}__{embedder} collection (no prefix for corpus_id="default").
archSection.table2Row3Role: BM25 sparse index with ru/be analyzers. Merged with Qdrant via RRF/weighted fusion.
archSection.table2Row4Role: Knowledge graph (document sections → edges). N-hop traversal from Qdrant seed documents.
archSection.table2Row5Role: LLM answer generation. NaivePipeline → generator.generate(prompt, sources).
archSection.tier1Desc: The RAG implements the platform's contract directly: POST / → {answer, sources[], trace?}. Maximum diagnostics (stage_trace, pre_rerank_source_refs, corpus_id routing). The reference RAG server dogfoods this contract.
archSection.tier2DescPart2: ) + response_mapping (JSONPath). No code required on the RAG side. corpus_id is always appended as a fallback field, even if the template doesn't include it.
archSection.tier3Desc: core/sdk.py: wrap_retriever/wrap_generator — a few lines of Python for RAGs too irregular for tier 2 (pagination, multi-call, custom auth, streaming).
archSection.whatBundledRagUsesHeading: What the bundled RAG uses (bundled reference impl.)
archSection.whatPlatformUsesHeading: What the platform itself uses — independent of the RAG
archSection.whatPlatformUsesParagraph: The platform connects to Qdrant and Neo4j directly for corpus inspection and diagnostics — this is not RAG retrieval, but the platform's own tooling. Right now the connections are hardcoded via env vars; the next step is making them configurable per-RAG, since external RAGs use their own instances.

bundleSection.anchorHeading: An anchor names content, not a position
bundleSection.anchorPara1: A chunk identifier is derived from a position in the index, so re-indexing can quietly change what it points at. An anchor instead names the source unit, the structural path, a hash of the normalised text and the quote itself.
bundleSection.anchorPara2: A recipient that chunked differently still finds the right unit, and is told so. Anchors that matched nothing are listed separately: a bundle that silently applies half of itself is worse than one that says so.
bundleSection.diagramCaption: Resolution happens once at load, not per query. That is exactly what separates the bundle from the retired mechanism, which reached into the platform's database on every question.
bundleSection.lead: A fix bundle is a self-contained, versioned document that a served system loads at startup. That is how a correction reaches it while the platform never sits in the path of its requests.
bundleSection.noCallback: no call to the platform at query time
bundleSection.thresholdCallout: If the two sets of examples overlap, no threshold exists, and that is said plainly. Returning a "best compromise" would hide that the mechanism cannot be used under those conditions at all.
bundleSection.thresholdHeading: A procedure instead of a number
bundleSection.thresholdPara1: A similarity threshold is not portable between systems. The distribution of cosine similarity depends on the embedding model, so a value that is strict under one model is permissive under another.
bundleSection.thresholdPara2: The bundle therefore carries a procedure rather than a number: examples that must match, examples that must not, and how to compute it. The recipient derives the threshold with its own model.
bundleSection.whereHeading: Where it is in the interface
bundleSection.wherePara1: The "Fix bundle" button in the judgments page toolbar. It reports the entry count, the format version and the number of calibration pairs, and the document itself is copyable in full.

configSection.graphRagDesc: Select the graph_hybrid retriever → the graph pipeline: the graph is built into Neo4j during ingest, and multi-hop traversal uses Cypher. Shows up as graph_ms / n_graph stages in the trace.

configSection.reproducibilityRest: enabling a step changes the config hash and observably changes the result; configurations without new fields keep the same hash, so historical runs stay comparable.

deepDiagnosticsSection.lead: Health (above) covers fast, deterministic checks. This section covers 4 independent LLM-judge sources, run on demand (Data → Health → "Deep diagnostics"), not automatically — each one makes one LLM call per question/chunk, so it's slow.
deepDiagnosticsSection.ragasDesc: context_precision / context_recall / answer_relevancy — the same RAG triad, but a different library and prompts, checked against a selected control set (10 questions, see "on demand" above).

Known limitation: razdel is trained on a limited set of languages, and a document in a language outside that set segments worse. No separate fallback was written: such a document is already linguistically isolated, which the graph clustering shows.
deepDiagnosticsSection.truLensDesc: RAG triad: context_relevance / groundedness / answer_relevance — calls the LiteLLM provider's feedback functions directly, without full TruLens app-instrumentation/dashboard (we only need the three numbers).
deepDiagnosticsSection.whyFourRest: DeepEval, Ragas, TruLens, and the chunk-coherence judge measure similar but not identical things, using different prompts and (generally) different judge models. Disagreement between their scores isn't a platform bug — it's a normal "LLM judges disagree" signal, and the disagreement itself shows how much you should trust any single judge's opinion in isolation. We deliberately chose not to merge them into one metric — the numbers are shown side by side.

diagnosisSection.causeHeading: The cause of a retrieval failure
diagnosisSection.causePara1: A "retrieval failure" verdict names a layer, not a fault. Four different situations hide under it, and they call for opposite actions: tuning the ranking is pointless when the document is not in the index at all.
diagnosisSection.causePara2: The platform separates them from evidence the run already stored. It looks at whether the expected reference resolved in the index, how many chunks the unit it names consists of, and where those chunks landed in a wide candidate list.
diagnosisSection.causePara3: When the presence of the source in the index could not be established, the cause is named "not established" and the lever becomes checking the index. That is more honest than picking one of the four: a wrongly named cause sends somebody to fix the wrong thing.
diagnosisSection.causeRanking: Found, but not in the selection
diagnosisSection.fanCaption: One verdict, four situations. On the right is the lever each one points at: that is what makes it a conclusion rather than an observation.
diagnosisSection.lead: The layer diagnosis above says where a question failed. This section is about what happens next: why it failed, which work to do first, and what that work is worth — measured before anybody does it.
diagnosisSection.loopBack: the next run measures the result
diagnosisSection.loopCaption: The lap closes with a run, not with an impression. The acceptance verdict is judged over the very questions the prescription named in advance.
diagnosisSection.loopPara1: The mechanisms form one loop, and each link is verifiable on its own. A run yields evidence, evidence yields a cause, the cause and the question count yield an order of work, the counterfactual yields the expected payoff, and the prescription hands all of it to whoever will do the fixing.
diagnosisSection.loopPara2: One lap on a real corpus went like this: the cause pointed at ranking, the counterfactual predicted twenty-three additional questions, changing the context size delivered exactly twenty-three, and acceptance judged the fix carried out.
diagnosisSection.payoffPara1: The candidate window and the context size are separate. The candidate window is how many candidates retrieval considers; the context size is how many of them reach the model.
diagnosisSection.payoffPara2: This lets the platform answer "what would a different context size have given" from a stored run without repeating it. It looks at the rank the expected source held for each question and counts how many questions each cut-off would have closed.
diagnosisSection.payoffPara3: The number of questions no context size would have closed — because their source never appeared at all — is reported separately. Without it the remainder would read as a tuning problem when it is a data-loading one.
diagnosisSection.priorityCallout: Beside the list stands the share of failures that share a cause with at least one other. It is there because the list looks equally actionable whether the failures generalise or every one of them is its own isolated case.
diagnosisSection.priorityPara1: Thirty failures are not thirty tasks. Failures group into (cause, document) pairs, and each such task carries the number of questions that would close if it were done.
diagnosisSection.priorityPara2: That number is what makes tasks comparable. A single per-question verdict has nothing to be compared against, while "twelve questions come down to one manual, three come down to three different ones" already sets the order of work.

frontierSection.latencyCallout: An external run's time is measured by the platform and covers only handing the request over and receiving the answer. The remote system's own work is not included. Times are therefore comparable within one group and not across groups.
frontierSection.latencyPara1: This is measurement, not supposition: one pair of runs at equal quality gave 0.15 milliseconds for the external system against 24.5 seconds for the built-in one — a factor of a hundred and sixty thousand, explained entirely by what was being measured. Mixing the two groups into one ranking produced a confident recommendation to adopt the external system on speed nobody had measured.
frontierSection.lead: The trade-off frontier is the set of configurations where none is beaten by another on both quality and response time at once. The page starts nothing; it compares runs that already happened.
frontierSection.plotCaption: The points on the dashed line are the ones worth choosing between. The grey ones are beaten by one of them on both numbers, so there is nothing to choose them for.
frontierSection.plotFrontier: on the frontier: a real choice
frontierSection.readPara1: Reading down the frontier is reading the price of each further increment of quality. If moving from one point to the next buys two percent of quality and triples the time, that decision belongs to a person, not to the platform.
frontierSection.readPara2: The beaten configurations are shown on request rather than dropped. "Here are your choices" reads differently depending on how many were ruled out: two of three and two of twenty mean different degrees of confidence.
frontierSection.trustHeading: Can the measure itself be trusted
frontierSection.trustPara1: Choosing a configuration rests on a quality measure, so the measure itself needs checking. The platform compares it against reviewer verdicts on the same questions.
frontierSection.trustPara2: The two directions of disagreement are not summed into one number. A measure calling a bad answer good lets a regression ship; a measure calling a good answer bad only wastes an investigation. A single agreement rate would let the cheap error mask the expensive one.
frontierSection.trustPara3: Alongside it, the platform measures how quality depends on where the source sat in the context. Observations are grouped by position rather than reduced to one coefficient: the dependency is not linear, and the ends behave differently from the middle.

judgmentsSection.lead: A relevance judgment is a reviewer's statement about what is correct for one particular question. The reviewer names which chunks should have been retrieved and which should not.
judgmentsSection.leadPara2: A judgment changes nothing about how retrieval works. It records an observation rather than issuing an order. Its value is that three different things follow from that observation, each of which acts on every future question rather than only on similar ones.
judgmentsSection.whatHeading: What a chunk is and what a judgment is
judgmentsSection.whatPara1: A chunk is a passage of text a document is cut into when it enters the search index. Retrieval returns chunks, not whole documents.
judgmentsSection.whatPara2: A judgment consists of the wording of the question, a list of relevant chunks and a list of irrelevant ones. A note for a future reader is stored alongside, together with a pointer to the run and the feedback the judgment came from.
judgmentsSection.whatPara3: A judgment deliberately has no similarity threshold: it applies to the question it was made about and to no other. A similar wording is a different question, and the platform does not decide for the reader how similar counts as the same.
judgmentsSection.whatPara4: A judgment is stored in a versioned file, one per project and corpus pair. The platform's database plays no part, because a served system in production has no access to that database and should not need any.
judgmentsSection.usesPara1: The first use turns the judgment into a permanent test. The question joins a golden set and the relevant chunks become its expected sources. From then on, losing them is caught by the next run rather than by the next complaint.
judgmentsSection.usesPara2: The second use yields training material. A relevant and an irrelevant chunk under one question form a preference pair, a ready example for tuning ranking. Unlike a one-off override, tuned ranking also acts on questions nobody has asked yet.
judgmentsSection.usesPara3: The third use is finding a common cause. Several judgments pointing at the same kind of mistake reveal not separate failures but one cause worth removing outright.
judgmentsSection.usesDiagramCaption: One reviewer observation yields a test, a training example, and evidence about a cause.
judgmentsSection.formPara1: Choose the corpus the question belongs to. The list is filled from the corpora already registered in the project.
judgmentsSection.formPara2: Enter the wording of the question. If you arrived from feedback triage, it is already filled in.
judgmentsSection.formPara3: Find the chunks by searching their text and mark each one relevant or irrelevant. You do not need to know a chunk id by heart.
judgmentsSection.formPara4: The note is optional, but it helps a future reader understand why the reviewer ruled the way they did.
judgmentsSection.formPara5: A judgment naming no chunk at all is not saved, because it states nothing.
judgmentsSection.offHeading: Why a judgment does not change retrieval
judgmentsSection.offPara1: A judgment is a record of what is correct, not an edit to retrieval. Substituting results mid-request would mean the served system's answer depends on the platform being reachable, and changes silently when it is not.
judgmentsSection.offPara2: Scanning the records on every question also costs time — seventy-two milliseconds per thousand records — and such a substitution never reaches an external retrieval system at all: the platform does not stand in its path.
judgmentsSection.offPara3: So the substitution is off by default and is switched on only for a single run on the stand, to test an assumption. It never affects a user's answer under any circumstances.
judgmentsSection.triageDefinitionPara1: Feedback triage is the automatic classification of a reviewer's free-text comment explaining why a specific answer was judged wrong.
judgmentsSection.triageDefinitionPara2: Such a comment often contains more than one distinct complaint at once. Feedback triage splits the comment into separate, individually checkable parts.
judgmentsSection.triageDefinitionPara3: Each part is assigned to one of a predetermined set of mistake categories, for example: a citation points to the wrong location within an otherwise correct source, an answer is built from the wrong source document, an outdated version of a legal provision was used, an answer sounds plausible but does not actually follow from the material it was given.
judgmentsSection.triageDefinitionPara4: For each identified category the platform also suggests the most appropriate corrective action, called a lever, for example: load or re-index the document, change how it is split into chunks, widen the candidate window, bring the question's wording closer to the document's.
judgmentsSection.triageMechanicsPara1: The classification is performed by the platform's own language model.
judgmentsSection.triageMechanicsPara2: Before showing the result to a reviewer, the platform performs a separate check that uses no model at all. For every specific reference the model judged mentioned in the comment, it verifies whether that reference actually corresponds to one of the chunks really found by search for this question.
judgmentsSection.triageMechanicsPara3: A classification that raises doubt is marked as needing manual review. This happens when the model could not produce a parseable answer, identified no recognized mistake category, or reported low confidence in its own result.
judgmentsSection.triageUiPara1: The triage panel sits directly beneath the feedback-entry field on the detailed run-results page, next to the generated answer for the same question.
judgmentsSection.triageUiPara2: It becomes available as soon as at least one text feedback comment exists for the question, and offers a button to request classification.
judgmentsSection.triageUiPara3: The classification result is shown together with the identified mistake categories, the suggested lever, and three buttons: "Confirm", "Reject", and "Record a judgment". The last one opens the judgments page with the question already filled in.
judgmentsSection.triageUiPara4: The last of these takes the reviewer to the Pins page with the "Corpus", "Question text", and "Source feedback ID" fields already filled in.
judgmentsSection.triageNeverAppliesPara1: Feedback triage only ever proposes a classification and a lever. Neither the classification nor the suggested lever is ever applied automatically. A pin is created only by a separate, explicit action the reviewer takes on the Pins page.
judgmentsSection.confirmDiffHeading: Difference from the "Confirm reference answer" button
judgmentsSection.confirmDiffPara1: The "Confirm reference answer" button is placed in the same question row as the feedback panel. It has no effect on retrieval and changes nothing about how the system answers.
judgmentsSection.confirmDiffPara2: It updates the question's record in the golden set, confirming or correcting the reference answer and the list of expected sources for this specific question.
judgmentsSection.confirmDiffPara3: Such a record is used exclusively for later quality evaluation, meaning the comparison of future generated answers against the reference. It does not change the behavior of search or answer generation in any way.
judgmentsSection.confirmDiffPara4: A relevance judgment, by contrast, changes no existing record. It adds a new observation about which chunks should have been retrieved for a question and which should not, and from it a test, a training pair and evidence about a cause are derived. It does not change retrieval either — why is explained above, under "Why a judgment does not change retrieval".
judgmentsSection.confirmDiffPara5: Feedback triage determines which category a mistake belongs to, and the category determines what is worth recording: a relevance judgment if the problem lies in what search found, or confirming/correcting the reference answer if the problem lies in the golden set's own record.

marketSection.gapsCallout: The last three rows are what the platform lacks and others have: implicit judgements from user behaviour, an annotation queue, and a run on every code change. The first removes the main limit on judgements — a human writes them, so there are never many.
marketSection.heading: Where it stands among existing tools
marketSection.para1: The RAG evaluation field can measure and observe. Metric libraries score answer and retrieval quality; observability platforms receive a running application's traces and let you annotate them; optimisers launch runs themselves in search of the best settings; search relevance tools work with judgements about which document suits which query.
marketSection.para2: None of the ideas used here was invented from scratch. The difference is that the field answers the next question poorly: what exactly to go and fix, in what order, and what it will buy. Only the rows that separate the classes are below; the full table of thirty-five functions is in the report.
marketSection.para3: The second line of difference is the stance toward somebody else's system. Most tools assume the evaluator owns what is evaluated. Here the opposite is assumed, and the prescription, the fix bundle and pulling traces rather than receiving them all follow from it.

prescriptionSection.acceptanceCallout: Acceptance uses the same definition of "this question is fine" as the regression guard. A separate definition would let the two mechanisms disagree about the same pair of runs.
prescriptionSection.acceptancePara1: After the fix a second run is made, and the platform compares it with the first over the very questions the prescription named in advance.
prescriptionSection.acceptancePara2: The verdict lists the questions fixed, those still failing and those that got worse. The last group matters most: a fix that closed ten questions and broke three looks successful in the averages.
prescriptionSection.contentPara1: Panels for reading and the same document as plain text for handing over. Both are derived from one server response, so they cannot disagree about a number.
prescriptionSection.contentPara2: Each fix carries the list of questions it will be judged on, fixed at the moment the document was written. A criterion the recipient can widen or narrow afterwards is not a criterion.
prescriptionSection.contentPara3: A separate part states what the system under test does not report, together with what its owner would change to make it reportable. A gap nobody can act on is a complaint rather than a finding.
prescriptionSection.lead: A prescription is the document the platform hands to the owner of the system under test. It exists because the person who will do the fixing is often not the person looking at the platform, and cannot open it.
prescriptionSection.whereHeading: Where it is in the interface
prescriptionSection.wherePara1: The "Prescription" tab on the run page, directly after "Diagnostics". The copy button yields the whole document in the form it can be sent in.
prescriptionSection.whyHeading: Why a score is not enough
prescriptionSection.whyPara1: A number like "quality 0.42" does not say what to do. The owner of an external system receives a score they can act on in no way, and the conversation turns into an argument about measurement methodology instead of one about a specific document.
prescriptionSection.whyPara2: Instead of a score, the prescription carries a list of fixes, each naming a cause, a lever, the document affected, a question count and examples. That is something one can work from without access to the platform.

problemsSection.problem11Title: The corpus silently loses sections when exported to separate files
problemsSection.problem12Cause: Inserted sections render as "Section 468 1", with a space instead of a period after the HTML-to-Markdown conversion. The regular expression captured only "468", and the second file "468 1" was written under the same name 468.txt, overwriting the first
problemsSection.problem12Fix: Normalise every separator in the section number — space, dash, period — to a period BEFORE forming the file name. The converter compares its written counter against the actual file count on disk after the run, and a mismatch signals a collision
problemsSection.problem12Symptom: After conversion there are fewer files than parsed sections, e.g. 7336 files instead of 7658, with not a single error in the log
problemsSection.problem12Title: The corpus converter overwrites sections with "superscript" numbers
problemsSection.problem13Cause: Bucketing chunks by keyword ignores frequency: words common to the whole subject area appear in thousands of chunks, and one such bucket produces N×(N−1)/2 edges. On a small corpus of three or four thousand nodes the problem does not show up
problemsSection.problem13Fix: apoc.periodic.iterate for batched transactions plus a dynamic frequency threshold (excluding keywords appearing in > 50 chunks) instead of a hardcoded stop list — adapts to any corpus's vocabulary
problemsSection.problem13Symptom: link_related() either runs out of memory (OOM on a single giant transaction) or creates an abnormal number of edges (14.7M edges over 31K nodes)
problemsSection.problem13Title: The Neo4j graph gets noisy when linking on shared keywords over a large corpus
problemsSection.problem14Cause: Docker Desktop on Mac keeps a separate fixed-size virtual disk (overlay fs) — the transaction logs from creating and then deleting millions of edges filled that disk, not the host
problemsSection.problem14Fix: Run docker exec <container> df -h / — check FROM INSIDE the container, not df -h on the host. docker system prune -f frees space in the VM; then docker restart the container that went down
problemsSection.problem14Symptom: Neo4j fails with "No space left on device" and asks for a restart, even though the host disk is nearly empty
problemsSection.problem14Title: The Docker Desktop VM disk fills up during mass edge create+delete in Neo4j
problemsSection.problem15Cause: The new-run form had no corpus_id field at all — ExperimentConfig silently accepted the default, regardless of which question set was chosen. A dataset↔corpus_id mismatch was invisible in the form
problemsSection.problem15Fix: Added a "Corpus" field to the new-run form (a datalist of known corpus_id values, synced to the default question set by default) — check recall@k grouped by question group (per document); a sharp 0.0 on part of a group hints at a corpus_id mismatch
problemsSection.problem15Symptom: retrieval_recall_at_k = 0 on most questions in a new golden set, even though the corpus is loaded and visible in the corpus_id dropdown (Data → Corpus → Content/Health/Graph)
problemsSection.problem15Title: A new run silently searches the wrong corpus
problemsSection.problem16Cause: The large communities — 61 of 1746, holding most of the nodes — each contain 12 to 27 different documents at once, with the dominant source's share usually between 0.1 and 0.45. Clusters form from shared frequent keywords between documents rather than from semantic closeness. Good modularity does not mean the discovered structure is meaningful
problemsSection.problem16Fix: Before trusting GraphRAG links on a new corpus, run the "Graph" tab and check distinct_source_count/dominant_source_share for the large communities. Heavy source mixing is a signal that RELATED's weighting/filtering (currently a binary match on at least one keyword after frequency cutoff) needs tightening, not that the current graph signal should be trusted as-is
problemsSection.problem16Symptom: Community detection (Leiden, "Graph" tab) reports plausible modularity (0.52) and non-trivial clusters — it looks like real structure
problemsSection.problem16Title: GraphRAG links (RELATED) look structured visually but are mostly noise
problemsSection.problem1Cause: Stub embedder: the corpus was indexed with random vectors. Bug: if use_real_model instead of if self._use_real_model
problemsSection.problem1Fix: Check the log for "Loading weights: 100%". If it's missing, run make ingest with USE_REAL_BGE_M3=true
problemsSection.problem1Symptom: The model finds nothing relevant for any question
problemsSection.problem1Title: All answers say: "The provided documents don't contain this information"
problemsSection.problem2Cause: chunk_id was generated via uuid4() — every ingest added new documents
problemsSection.problem2Fix: Deterministic chunk_id = sha256(source:strategy:start:end)[:32] — already fixed. For an old index: DELETE /chunks_*
problemsSection.problem2Symptom: After a repeated make ingest, the document count multiplied
problemsSection.problem2Title: Duplicates in OpenSearch (doc count is 4x expected)
problemsSection.problem3Cause: qwen3:8b thinking mode: the model spends the entire num_predict budget inside <think>...</think>, running out before answering
problemsSection.problem3Fix: "think": false in the Ollama request — already fixed in adapters/ollama_generator.py
problemsSection.problem3Symptom: Every answer in the run is an empty string
problemsSection.problem4Cause: The questions contain a phrase common to the entire corpus, such as the name of the subject area itself, and BM25 scores highly on every source containing it
problemsSection.problem4Fix: Use hybrid-rrf: dense retrieval finds the right source by meaning rather than by frequent word overlap
problemsSection.problem4Symptom: The top sparse result is a source whose title carries that common phrase and has nothing to do with the question's topic
problemsSection.problem4Title: BM25 returns sources unrelated to the question
problemsSection.problem5Cause: _save() and _get_results() were sync def but called Motor's async methods
problemsSection.problem5Fix: Change them to async def and update every call site to use await
problemsSection.problem5Symptom: TypeError: object NoneType can't be used in 'await' expression
problemsSection.problem5Title: MongoDB Motor async used in a sync router
problemsSection.problem6Cause: Before the deterministic chunk_id was introduced, every make ingest added new copies of chunks. top-k=5 returned 5 copies of the same chunk
problemsSection.problem6Fix: A deterministic chunk_id plus dedup on chunk_text already fix this. For old indexes: delete the collection and reindex
problemsSection.problem6Symptom: The same text appears 3–4 times in the prompt context, and the model answers "tautologically"
problemsSection.problem6Title: Duplicates in the top-k context across repeated ingestions
problemsSection.problem7Cause: _traverse() and _split_text() didn't pass through doc.source — they used only doc.doc_id. sha256 collisions occur when source is empty
problemsSection.problem7Fix: Added a source parameter to _traverse and _split_text, passed through from doc.source in chunk()
problemsSection.problem7Symptom: chunk.metadata[source] is empty; chunk_id collides across chunks from different documents
problemsSection.problem8Cause: Answers were found by sparse retrieval, but the chunk holds only a section header with no substantive text: structure_aware was creating header-only chunks
problemsSection.problem8Fix: Check structural_path in source_refs: if they're all from section[HEADING], the strategy is splitting on headers only. Increase min_chars or use sentence/paragraph for such documents
problemsSection.problem8Symptom: reference_overlap is lower than expected despite a correct corpus
problemsSection.problem8Title: Retrieval returns unsuitable sources when the sparse weight is low
problemsSection.problem9Cause: doc.structure was never populated in _read_file() — no production parser building a DocumentNode from a file actually existed
problemsSection.problem9Fix: A structure parser inside a domain pack plus the --structure CLI flag that selects it (for example `--structure manual_section` from domain_packs/manuals). Locked in with a unit test on a real corpus file rather than a hand-written fixture
problemsSection.problem9Symptom: structural_path is "root" for every chunk, with boundaries falling exactly every 512 characters mid-word — despite --strategy structure_aware
problemsSection.problem9Title: structure_aware silently degrades to fixed windows on every real ingest

productionSection.arrowFix: the fix goes back into the running system
productionSection.boxCoverage: Coverage: what the set does not speak to
productionSection.candidateCallout: A deployment with logging switched off is reported in its own words. Otherwise it is indistinguishable from a system with no traffic, and the two must be told apart: the first is a deployment oversight, the second is information about users.
productionSection.candidatePara1: A record says what happened. Whether it was a mistake is a human judgement nobody has made yet, so what is collected is filed as material for review rather than as a stream of complaints.
productionSection.coverageHeading: What the golden set does not cover
productionSection.coveragePara1: Each production query is given its similarity to the nearest question in the set. The nearest specifically: a query is covered when some question resembles it, and averaging over a large set would drag every value toward zero.
productionSection.coveragePara2: The uncovered share is shown together with the decile distribution, because the shape matters as much as the share. A set covering most queries poorly and a set covering most well while missing a few produce similar shares and call for opposite work.
productionSection.lead: A production query is a question a live person asked a running system. Everything else the platform sees was thought up in advance, and a question nobody anticipated cannot fail a test that does not exist.
productionSection.loopCaption: The platform reaches out to the system, never the other way round. A system that sent records itself would have to know the platform's address and be up at the same time.
productionSection.promoteHeading: From a failure to a test
productionSection.promotePara1: The question text is taken verbatim. A tidied-up paraphrase would test a question nobody asked, and the whole value of a real query is that it is not what anyone would have invented.
productionSection.promotePara2: The reference answer is written by hand and never taken from the log: the system's answer is precisely what is being disputed, and copying it into the reference would enshrine the failure as the standard. Adding the same query twice is refused while the question it became still exists.
productionSection.pullPara1: The platform reaches the log endpoint itself, and does so when an operator asks. The reverse order would introduce a dependency of the running system on the platform that must not exist.
productionSection.pullPara2: A pleasant consequence follows: a system that has never heard of the platform is unaffected by its existence. Fetching again over an overlapping window creates no duplicates, because the log is a ring and overlap is the normal case.

purposeSection.calloutInfoPart1: Every platform feature (Pipeline Trace, MongoDB history, run diagnostics) grew out of a real debugging incident — see the "Common Problems" section and
purposeSection.calloutWarnPart1: The architecture is built around a registry pattern (swappable chunker/embedder/retriever/reranker) and
purposeSection.calloutWarnPart3: — any combination of components is reproducible and comparable. The subject area lives in a domain pack, not in the platform: the platform's goal is debugging
purposeSection.lead: The platform is a tool for iteratively debugging and comparing RAG configurations on your own data — not a finished product with one hardcoded pipeline.
purposeSection.mainUserDesc: An engineer/researcher configuring and validating a RAG before handing it to end users. Not a chatbot reader — someone who runs experiments, inspects traces and metrics, changes a single component (chunker, reranker, prompt) and compares it against the previous run.
purposeSection.painDesc: RAG systems are a black box where silent degradation is easy to miss (stub embeddings, duplicate entries in the index, thinking mode eating the whole budget, BM25 ranking on stop words). Without tracing/comparison, the only way to catch it is digging through logs after a user complaint.

realmSection.lead: A realm is a separate workspace: its own corpus, its own control-question sets, its own prompts, its own runs and its own infrastructure.
realmSection.whatIs: Everything visible on the screens belongs to the selected realm and to it alone. Two realms on one host share the running Qdrant, OpenSearch and Ollama, but they do not share data: a run made in one will not appear in the other's list, and a corpus loaded into one is not found by a search in the other.
realmSection.switching: The switcher sits in the top-left corner under the platform name. Below the realm's name is its identifier — the name it is written under in addresses and in exports. The name can be changed, the identifier cannot, and it is the identifier that ends up in the link: every screen's address carries “?realm=”, so a link to a run can be handed to someone else and it opens in the same realm.
realmSection.calloutScope: Switching realms changes the contents of every screen at once, chat included. An empty list of runs after switching is not lost data — it is a different realm.
realmSection.transferHeading: Moving a realm to another host
realmSection.transfer1: A realm exports into a single “causa-realm/v1” file: settings, resources, control-question sets with their questions, prompts and presets. Loading it on another host shows a reconciliation first — how much of what will appear and what collides by name — and writes nothing until it is confirmed.
realmSection.transfer2: A name collision aborts the whole load by default rather than quietly overwriting: a realm assembled a week earlier is worth more than the convenience of one button. Passwords and keys are left out of the export — placeholders stand in their place, and they are entered again after loading.
realmSection.calloutCorpus: Corpus content is not part of the file: it is tens of thousands of chunks in Qdrant and OpenSearch. What travels is the reference to the corpus; the documents themselves are ingested again on the new host.
realmSection.metrics1: Each realm has its own list of the metrics it is judged by. The list decides which columns stand in the runs table and which numbers are shown in the band on the run page and in the overview.
realmSection.metrics2: The list is set once and governs all of those places at once. Its first entry counts as the principal one: the overview picks the best run by it, and the trade-off frontier is measured by it until another is chosen.

shellSection.lead: The shell is what surrounds the screens: the command palette, notifications and the view switches. Anything done with the mouse can be done from the keyboard.
shellSection.palette1: The palette opens with ⌘K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux) and holds the jumps to every screen, creating a run, switching theme and colour palette, and switching language. You type any part of a name rather than the exact one.
shellSection.palette2: One and the same command entry feeds the palette, the shortcut sheet and the menu's bottom bar: the list is not duplicated anywhere, so a new command appears in all three at once. Shortcuts read the physical key rather than the letter printed on it — otherwise they would stop working on a non-Latin layout.
shellSection.notify1: The bell beside the platform name shows events derived from the same data the screens request anyway: a run finished, a run failed, a corpus ingest completed, a resource stopped answering, a regression against the baseline appeared, new production queries were collected.
shellSection.calloutNotify: Notifications have no server side, and the event is the transition rather than the response: “the run finished” appears at the moment it stopped being in progress, not on every poll that found it finished.
shellSection.view1: The view icon switches the light and dark themes and five colour palettes; the globe switches the language, with the current one's code beside it. The choice is remembered in the browser and applies to everything, charts and diagrams included: their colours come from the same variables rather than being set separately.

packsSection.lead: A domain pack is a pluggable set of rules for one subject area: what a section heading looks like, how a question about a procedure differs from one about safety, what to say when there is nothing to stand on.
packsSection.whatIs: The platform does not know any of that and should not: its core is neutral to any subject area, and a test enforces that rather than a convention. A pack supplies the missing knowledge, and it is enabled per realm, on the Domain packs page.
packsSection.where1: Two places are scanned: this build’s domain_packs/, which holds the examples that ship with the platform, and any directory named in the CAUSA_DOMAIN_PACKS environment variable.
packsSection.where2: A pack carrying your own subject area belongs in the second: it holds your domain’s vocabulary — refusal wording, error classes, the parsing of your headings — and has no place in the platform’s shared repository. If its id collides with an example, yours wins.
packsSection.add1: A pack is code. A directory, a pack.yaml manifest, and a module with register(registry, settings) that puts components into the registry:
packsSection.add2: The interface cannot create a pack, deliberately: a pack brings executable rules, not a row in a table. The Domain packs page shows what was found and enables it for a realm; the enabling is stored in the database, the pack itself in files.
packsSection.calloutExternal: A pack plugs into the platform’s own built-in pipeline: its routing, masks and refusal run inside its own RAG. It has nothing to do with an external RAG over HTTP — that system has its own logic, and the platform only measures it.
packsSection.calloutRestart: Packs load once, when the gateway starts. A new pack, or an edit to one, is visible after a restart; enabling and disabling on the page is not — that is read on every request.

answerRelevance.hint: Cosine similarity between the answer and the QUESTION itself (not the reference answer) — whether the model answers what was actually asked, independent of correctness. A deterministic analog of deepeval's AnswerRelevancy.

answerSimilarity.hint: Cosine similarity between the answer's and the reference answer's embeddings. Robust to paraphrasing.

citationNumberCoverage.hint: Share of article/section numbers from the golden source specifically (article_refs) that actually appear in the answer text (domain-neutral — not tied to the word "Article", see core/citation.py). A low value alongside high Retrieval Recall means the model garbles the number when citing, even though it found the right source. Absent if the corpus has no extractable structural markers, or if no retrieved chunk matched the reference (recall@k=0).

contextSupport.hint: Maximum (not average) cosine similarity between the answer and any one of the retrieved chunks.

correctRefusal.hint: Share of questions where the system correctly decided whether to answer or refuse (across ALL questions — the only metric independent of whether the corpus actually contains a source).

groundedInCorrectSource.hint: Cosine similarity between the answer and specifically the chunk(s) matching the golden article_refs — not the maximum across all chunks, unlike Context Support. Absent if the required article wasn't retrieved.

legacyJaccard.hint: The old Jaccard metric — not comparable with newer runs.

preRerankRecallAtK.hint: Recall@K over the list before the reranker. Present only when a reranker is active — lets you tell "retrieval didn't find it" apart from "retrieval found it, rerank dropped it".
preRerankRecallAtK.label: Recall@K before rerank

retrievalAveragePrecision.hint: Retrieval ranking quality: accounts for the relevant article's position within the top-k, not just its presence. A deterministic analog of deepeval's ContextualPrecision (no LLM judge).

retrievalPrecisionAtK.hint: Share of relevant articles among the retrieved top-k (deduplicated by article).

retrievalRecallAtK.hint: Share of the required articles (per the golden article_refs) found in the top-k. Answerable questions only. A pure retrieval signal — independent of the generator.

baselineDense.description: Pure dense retrieval via Qdrant, no hybridization and no rerank. The baseline for comparing all other configurations.

graphragGrounding.description: Graph retrieval with claim-level checking of the answer against the context. Useful for analytical multi-hop questions where it matters to avoid linking unrelated facts (hallucinations).

graphragMultihop.description: Graph retrieval on top of Neo4j: links chunks via adjacency and shared entities. Stronger on questions that require connecting several articles/sections (multi-hop). Requires ingest with USE_GRAPH=true.

graphragRerank.description: Graph retrieval + top-k reordering by a local cross-encoder. The graph provides connected context, the reranker surfaces the most relevant chunks. Requires the [graph] and [reranker] extras.

highRecall.description: Increased top-k for maximum context coverage. Useful for analytical questions that need several articles.

hybridRrf.description: Dense + sparse merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Balances semantic and lexical similarity.

hybridWeighted.description: Weighted merge of dense + sparse — prioritizes the dense score. Good for a domain corpus with settled terminology.

findingAction.embedder_unverified: Read the run's recall against its reference sources: a corpus indexed by a stub model retrieves at chance.
findingAction.stub_embedder: Re-index the corpus with the real embedding model switched on.
findingAction.duplicates: Check that chunk_id is deterministic, then drop the collection and re-index.
findingAction.header_only: Raise min_chars, or switch to sentence or paragraph chunking.
findingAction.bm25_dominance: Compare the two halves' own recall separately before changing the merge.
findingAction.empty_answers: Check corpus coverage, and whether the model's thinking mode is consuming the num_predict budget.
findingAction.incorrect_refusals: Read each question's answerability class (core.eval.answerability). A question with no reference sources is out of scope and should be refused.
findingAction.layer_bottleneck: Open the individual questions carrying this verdict on the run page to see the specific failures and decide what to fix.
findingAction.unverified_coverage: Check that the index for this corpus is reachable, then re-run to get verified classes.
findingAction.undeclared_metric: Declare each metric beside its name, saying what it computes and over which questions, so the name can be checked against it.
findingAction.aggregate_disagrees: Compare what the run wrote with what a read of it returns; a question lost on the way out moves the aggregate and leaves everything else looking correct.
findingAction.chunk_id_collision: Check how the identifier is derived at load time: a source path missing from the derivation collapses fragments of different documents onto one value.
findingAction.unmeasured_stage_cost: Record a duration for every stage the pipeline runs, so its price can be compared with the gain it is kept for.

config.chunkingStrategyHint: How documents were split into chunks at indexing time (fixed/structure_aware/sentence/paragraph) — determines the text boundaries retrieval sees.
config.configHashHint: A deterministic hash of the whole config (core/experiment/config.py) — two runs with the same hash are guaranteed comparable; a different hash means at least one pipeline parameter differs.
config.controlQuestionsHint: The golden set (eval/golden/*.jsonl) the metrics were computed on — question, reference answer and expected sources for each item.
config.corpusIdHint: Which indexed corpus (namespace in Qdrant/OpenSearch/Neo4j) was used for retrieval — "default" if no corpus was explicitly specified.
config.durationHint: How long the run actually took from start to finishing all questions.
config.embedderHint: The model used to compute vectors for dense search in Qdrant (e.g. bge_m3) — must match the embedder that indexed the Corpus ID.
config.generatorHint: Shows the actual model that generated the answers (e.g. qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M) — determines answer quality and style, doesn't affect retrieval. Runs from before this fix didn't persist the model name — the adapter kind (ollama/vllm/stub) is shown instead.
config.heading: Configuration
config.implementationHint: Built-in — the pipeline was assembled and run by the platform in-process (white-box, full trace). External — the request went out over HTTP to a third-party RAG service; diagnostics are complete only if the external service itself returned stage_trace/sources.
config.mergeHint: How dense and sparse results were merged in hybrid pipelines — rrf (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) or weighted (weighted score sum). Doesn't apply to graph/naive pipelines.
config.name: Name
config.nameHint: The run's name, set at launch (the "Name" field in the new-run form) — doesn't affect the pipeline itself, only how it's displayed in the list.
config.pipelineHint: Which registered pipeline_id served the requests — determines which retriever/reranker actually took part (naive/hybrid_rrf/hybrid_weighted/graph/configurable). See core/pipeline.py.
config.promptHint: The generator's system prompt template active at run time (core/prompt_store.py) — determines the model's instructions (citation format, answer language, etc.). Prompt text is hidden by default — reveal it with the button below.
config.questionsHint: How many questions from the golden set were actually run (may be fewer than the full set if the run form set a limit).
config.rerankerHint: The cross-encoder that re-ranked the top-k after the initial retrieval (cross_encoder_local/cross_encoder) — "not used" if reranking wasn't enabled in the config.
config.seedHint: The random-number-generator seed used for reproducibility — the same config plus the same seed should produce identical answers on a repeat run.
config.topKHint: How many chunks were passed to the generator's context after retrieval (and rerank, if any) — a higher value gives more context but also more noise.

answerRelevance.hint: Cosine similarity between the answer and the question itself — whether the model answers what was asked, independent of content correctness. A deterministic analog of deepeval's AnswerRelevancy.

answerSimilarity.hint: Cosine similarity between the answer's and reference's embeddings. Robust to paraphrasing — unlike the old Jaccard metric.

citationNumberCoverage.hint: Share of article numbers from the golden source (article_refs) that actually appear in the answer text — checks whether the model garbles the number when citing, even though it found the right source (core/citation.py). Absent if the corpus has no extractable structural markers, or if no retrieved chunk matched the reference.

contextSupport.hint: Maximum (not average!) cosine similarity between the answer and any one of the retrieved chunks — is there at least one chunk the answer resembles.

correctRefusal.hint: Share of questions where the system correctly decided whether to answer or refuse. Computed over ALL questions (answerable or not) — the only metric independent of whether the corpus contains a source.

groundedInCorrectSource.hint: Cosine similarity between the answer and specifically the chunk(s) matching the golden article_refs — not the maximum across all chunks, unlike Context Support. Distinguishes "the answer resembles the right content" from "the answer is grounded in the specific required article".

preRerankRecallAtK.hint: Recall@K over the list before the reranker (present only when a reranker is active). A gap from Retrieval Recall@K shows the reranker dropped the required article from the top-k.

retrievalAveragePrecision.hint: Retrieval ranking quality — accounts for the relevant article's position in the top-k, not just its presence (unlike Retrieval Precision@K). A deterministic analog of deepeval's ContextualPrecision.

retrievalPrecisionAtK.hint: Share of relevant articles among the retrieved top-k (deduplicated by article). A low value alongside high recall means the top-k is too noisy.

retrievalRecallAtK.hint: Share of the required articles (per the golden article_refs) found in the top-k. Computed on answerable questions only. A pure retrieval signal — independent of the generator.

rootCause.heading: Cause of the retrieval failure:
rootCause.leverIngest: Check document ingestion. The expected source is not in the index, so ranking work will change nothing.
rootCause.leverRanking: Raise the selection size or tune ranking. The source is found, but stays outside the selected set.
rootCause.leverChunking: Compare the chunking against the expected ref. The unit spans several chunks and none is close to the question. Either the chunking is too fine or the ref names too broad a section.
rootCause.leverVerifyIndex: Establish whether the source is in the index. Until that is known no cause can be named, and changing anything is premature.
rootCause.leverVocabulary: Close the wording gap. The unit is a single chunk, so splitting is not at fault; the question's words and the document's terms diverge.
rootCause.leverChunkingOrVocabulary: Check chunking and the wording gap. Which of the two it is cannot be established from this run.

frontierPage.dominatedIntro: Each is beaten by some other configuration on both quality and time, so there is nothing to choose it for. They are listed because "here are your choices" reads very differently depending on how many configurations were ruled out.
frontierPage.emptyBody: A run reaches this page once it has both the selected quality measure ({{metric}}) and a measured response time. A run missing either number is left out rather than placed at zero, where an unmeasured configuration would look like the cheapest good one.
frontierPage.intro: The trade-off frontier is the set of configurations where none is beaten by another on both quality and response time at once. A configuration beaten on both numbers cannot be chosen for any reason, and is left out. This page starts nothing; it compares runs that already happened.
frontierPage.latencyCaveatFull: An external run's time is measured by the platform and covers only handing the request over and receiving the answer. The remote system's own work is not included and stays invisible until that system reports a measurement of its own. Times are therefore comparable within one group and not across groups: one measured pair differed by a factor of 160,000 for this reason alone.
frontierPage.noRealm: Choose a Realm to see its runs.
frontierPage.title: Trade-off frontier
frontierPage.tokensExcludedFull: Some runs in this group carry no token counts, so the third axis took no part in the comparison. A run without counts would otherwise read as the cheapest of the set — the same mistake that keeps a run with no quality measure off the frontier entirely.
frontierPage.tokensExplain: The third axis is measured in tokens, not in money. Tokens are what the platform observes; money is tokens times a price it has no source for. A locally hosted model costs no money and plenty of compute, so a zero in currency for one and a real sum for another would put two different quantities on one axis. Multiply tokens by your own price to get money.

productionPage.collectDisabled: The system reports that its logging is switched off. That is not the same as having no traffic, and the two states have to be told apart by hand.
productionPage.collectIntro: The platform reaches the given address once and stores what comes back. Fetching again over an overlapping window creates no duplicates: a running system's log is a ring, so overlap is the normal case rather than an error.
productionPage.corpusListEmpty: This Realm has no registered corpora. The identifier can be typed by hand.
productionPage.corpusListFailed: The corpus list could not be fetched. The identifier can be typed by hand.
productionPage.coverageIntro: Each production query is given its similarity to the nearest question in the set. The nearest, not the average over the set: a query is covered when some question resembles it, and averaging over a large set would drag every value toward zero.
productionPage.coverageTitle: What the golden set does not cover
productionPage.decilesHint: The shape matters as much as the share. A set covering most queries poorly and a set covering most well while missing a few produce similar shares and call for opposite work.
productionPage.decilesTitle: Distribution of similarity to the nearest question in the set, by decile
productionPage.emptyBody: The platform fetches a running system's log when an operator asks it to. Give the log address and the collected queries appear here as candidates, not as complaints.
productionPage.emptyTitle: No queries for this corpus yet
productionPage.intro: A production query is a question a live person asked a running system. Everything else the platform sees was thought up in advance, and a question nobody anticipated cannot fail a test that does not exist. The platform reaches out to the system for its log and never waits for the system to come to it: otherwise that system would have to know the platform's address and be running at the same time.
productionPage.noRealm: Choose a Realm to work with its queries.
productionPage.noSources: Not one source was found. That on its own is the finding.
productionPage.pickCorpusBody: A query belongs to the corpus it was answered from, so the list appears once a corpus is selected above.
productionPage.promoteIntro: The question text is taken verbatim, as the person wrote it. A tidied-up paraphrase would test a question nobody asked, and the whole value of a real query is that it is not what anyone would have invented.
productionPage.promotionGone: This query was already turned into question {{id}}, but no such question remains in any set. It can be added again: the mark keeps the history, it does not forbid a repeat.
productionPage.referenceAnswerHint: Written by hand and never taken from the log: the system's answer is precisely what is being disputed, and copying it into the reference would enshrine the failure as the standard.
productionPage.refsHint: Comma-separated, optional. Without them the question still measures answer generation and refusal, and a reviewer may not yet know where the right source lives.
productionPage.selectHint: Choose a query on the left to see it in full.
productionPage.title: Production queries
productionPage.uncoveredHint: Furthest first: the query standing furthest from anything tested is the one most worth turning into a test. The list is capped in length; the share above counts every one.
productionPage.urlHint: The running system's own log endpoint. The platform does not guess it from a registration: a log may be served from a different host, and a guessed address would quietly collect nothing.
productionPage.allCovered: Every collected query is already covered by the set.
